passage: In the 1790s the physician Edward Jenner investigated a piece of rural folklore: that dairymaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease of cattle, seemed never to catch the far deadlier smallpox. Jenner argued that exposure to cowpox somehow protected a person against smallpox and that this protection could be transferred deliberately from one person to another. A historian of medicine wants to support the claim that Jenner's case rested on more than the folklore he started from.
question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historian's claim?

choices.text: Cowpox was widely known among rural dairy workers in eighteenth-century England as a mild illness caught from cattle.
Folk beliefs about the protective power of cowpox had circulated among dairy farmers for generations before Jenner began his work.
Smallpox was one of the most feared and lethal diseases in eighteenth-century Europe at the time Jenner was working.
Jenner deliberately exposed a healthy boy to material from a cowpox sore and later found that the boy did not contract smallpox when exposed to it.

explanation: Choice D is correct. The historian's claim is that Jenner's case rested on more than the folklore he started from. A deliberate test—exposing a person to cowpox and then finding that smallpox did not take hold—goes beyond the inherited belief and supplies evidence of the kind the claim says Jenner had. Choice D reports just such a test. Choices A and B restate the folklore and its currency, which is the very starting point the claim says Jenner moved past. Choice C establishes how dangerous smallpox was, important context but not evidence that Jenner's case went beyond folklore.
